$meta.note: Terms a player meets in the game that are not everyday words, each with a plain explanation. One entry per term; the Hindi edition translates this file and adds the textbook (NCERT) Hindi term where it differs from the everyday one. Drafted 24 November 2026 for review; not yet read by Shantanu or Kartik. Not yet drawn by any screen.

immuneSystem.meaning: Everything in the body that finds and destroys germs: the white blood cells, the antibodies they make, and the organs that make and house them.
immunity.meaning: Being protected against a disease, because the body can destroy it before it takes hold.
pathogen.meaning: Anything that causes disease when it gets into the body: a bacterium, a virus, a fungus, a parasite, or a toxin.
innate.meaning: The defences you are born with. They attack anything foreign at once, the same way every time: the Monocyte, the Neutrophil, the NK Cell, the Eosinophil and complement.
adaptive.meaning: The defences that learn. They take days to start, but they fit one germ exactly and remember it: the B-Cell, the Helper T-Cell and the Killer T-Cell.
antigen.meaning: A piece of a germ's surface that the immune system can recognise. An antibody fits one antigen the way a key fits one lock.
antibody.meaning: A Y-shaped protein the B-Cell makes. Its arms grip one antigen; its stem is a handle that phagocytes can hold. It can coat a germ, or neutralise it.
antigenClass.meaning: The game's six groups of antigen: ENV, NAK, EXB, ICB, TOX and EUK. An antibody of one class fits only pathogens of that class.
coat.meaning: To cover a germ in antibodies so that a phagocyte can grip and swallow it. Coating does not kill; it marks the target. The scientific word is opsonisation.
neutralise.meaning: To stop a virus or a toxin by binding antibodies to it, so it can no longer enter a cell or do harm.
phagocyte.meaning: A cell that eats: it wraps itself round a germ and digests it. The Monocyte, the Neutrophil and the resident macrophages are phagocytes.
engulf.meaning: What a phagocyte does: it swallows a germ whole and digests it. The scientific word is phagocytosis.
monocyte.meaning: A white blood cell that circulates in the blood and, in the tissues, becomes a macrophage: the big eater that swallows germs and shows their antigens to the adaptive cells.
macrophage.meaning: A large phagocyte that lives in the tissues. Every organ has resident macrophages of its own, with their own names: Kupffer cells in the liver, microglia in the brain.
neutrophil.meaning: The most numerous white blood cell, and the first to reach an infection. It swallows germs and can throw a NET.
net.meaning: Neutrophil extracellular trap: a sticky web of the neutrophil's own DNA, thrown out to trap and kill microbes around it. The neutrophil dies doing it.
bcell.meaning: The adaptive cell that makes antibodies. Each B-Cell makes antibodies against one antigen only.
helper.meaning: The adaptive cell that coordinates the others. It kills nothing itself; once primed, it makes the B-Cell, the Killer T-Cell and the Eosinophil work better.
killerT.meaning: The adaptive cell that destroys the body's own cells when a germ is hiding inside them. The scientific name is cytotoxic T cell.
nk.meaning: Natural killer cell: an innate cell that destroys infected cells without needing an antigen first. Fast, but less exact than the Killer T-Cell.
eosinophil.meaning: A white blood cell full of toxic granules, specialised against worms and parasites that are too big to swallow.
degranulate.meaning: To release all the toxic granules at once onto a worm. It kills, but it also harms the tissue around it.
complement.meaning: A set of proteins in the blood that coat germs by themselves and punch holes in them. Part of innate immunity.
antigenPresentation.meaning: When a phagocyte shows pieces of the germ it has eaten on its surface, so that the Helper T-Cell can see them and switch on the adaptive response.
priming.meaning: Switching on a Helper T-Cell by presenting an antigen to it. An unprimed Helper does nothing.
memory.meaning: After the body beats a disease, some B-Cells and T-Cells remain as memory cells. If the same disease returns, they destroy it at once.
memoryCells.meaning: Long-lived B-Cells and T-Cells that remember one disease and respond immediately when it returns.
vaccine.meaning: A harmless version or piece of a germ that gives the body memory of it, without the disease.
clonalSelection.meaning: How the body finds the one B-Cell, out of millions, whose antibody fits a new antigen, and copies it. It is why a first response to a new germ takes days.
affinityMaturation.meaning: After repeated exposure, the B-Cells' antibodies become a better and better fit for their antigen.
bacterium.meaning: A single-celled living microbe. Bacteria divide to multiply, and some release toxins.
virus.meaning: A tiny particle that can only multiply inside a living cell. Outside a cell it can be neutralised by antibodies; inside, only the Killer T-Cell or NK Cell can reach it.
enveloped.meaning: A virus wrapped in a piece of membrane stolen from the cell it came from, studded with spikes. Antibodies target the spikes.
naked.meaning: A virus with no envelope: a bare protein shell. Tough, and it survives on surfaces.
hidden.meaning: A pathogen living inside one of the body's own cells, out of reach of antibodies. Most are viruses; some are protozoa.
fungus.meaning: A microbe more like a plant cell than a bacterium: moulds and yeasts. Antibodies cannot coat it; phagocytes fight it.
parasite.meaning: An organism that lives on or in the body and feeds from it. In the game: protozoa such as the amoeba, and worms.
protozoa.meaning: Single-celled animals, such as the ones that cause malaria, amoebiasis and sleeping sickness.
worm.meaning: A parasitic worm, such as a roundworm or tapeworm. Far too big for any cell to swallow; the Eosinophil attacks it from outside.
toxin.meaning: A poison made by a bacterium. It is not alive, so no cell can eat it; only antitoxin antibodies stop it.
antitoxin.meaning: Antibodies that bind a toxin and make it harmless.
venom.meaning: The poison a snake or scorpion injects. It acts in minutes, faster than the body can make antibodies.
antivenom.meaning: Ready-made antibodies against a venom, raised in horses and given as an injection. The only treatment for a serious bite.
passiveImmunity.meaning: Protection from antibodies made somewhere else: antivenom, or a mother's antibodies in her baby. It works at once but does not last, and the body learns nothing.
lymph.meaning: Lymph is fluid that drains from the tissues through its own vessels. Lymph nodes are the stations along them where immune cells gather and meet antigens.
lymphatics.meaning: The vessels that carry lymph. Immune cells travel along them; so can germs.
spleen.meaning: An organ that filters the blood and removes bacteria from it. Without it, bacteria in the blood multiply faster.
boneMarrow.meaning: The tissue inside bones where every blood cell, including every white blood cell, is made.
integrity.meaning: In the game, how much damage an organ can still take. At zero the organ fails and the body is lost.
immunosuppression.meaning: A weakened immune response, from stress, malnutrition, some illnesses or some medicines.
neutropenia.meaning: Too few neutrophils in the blood.
lymphopenia.meaning: Too few lymphocytes (B-Cells and T-Cells) in the blood.
cytokineStorm.meaning: An immune response so strong that the inflammation itself damages the body.
antigenicVariation.meaning: When a germ changes its surface so that the antibodies made against it no longer fit. Sleeping sickness does this.
ade.meaning: When antibodies from an earlier infection help a related virus get into cells instead of stopping it. It is why a second dengue infection can be worse.
actionPoints.meaning: The game's measure of what the body can do in one turn. Every action costs some; unspent points are lost.
turn.meaning: One round of the game: new infections arrive, you command your cells, then the invaders spread.
spread.meaning: The part of each turn when the invaders act: they divide, hide, release toxins, feed, and advance one step toward the organs.
route.meaning: One of the six ways a germ enters the body: the nose, the gut, contact, a wound, a bite, or the blood.
resident.meaning: A macrophage that lives permanently in one organ and defends it. It never leaves that organ's branch.
